I'd keep this candidate out under part 2. The quote is on the page, but it only gives a ship date and a speed comparison for a chip platform. It doesn't say what the AI will do.

**1. Is the quote on the page?** Yes, word for word. The page is an Nvidia blog post titled "Keynote Wrap-Up: Turning Data Centers into 'AI Factories,'…", written by Brian Caulfield and dated March 22, 2022. The full sentence reads: "And [Huang announced Hyperion 9], featuring the coming DRIVE Atlan SoC for double the performance of the current DRIVE Orin-based architecture, which will ship starting in 2026." The run was right that these are the writer's words, not Huang's. The post is a company write-up of the keynote, not a transcript, so at best this would be a "pass, coverage only".

**2. Reading against the rule:**
- **Part 1 passes.** Huang has been Nvidia's co-founder and chief executive since 1993.
- **Part 2 fails.** The sentence says a self-driving hardware platform and its chip will be twice as fast as the current one and will ship from 2026. Nothing in it says what the self-driving AI will do or how far it will be deployed. Under the rule, a product shipping counts only when the words say something about what the AI will do or about its deployment, and a plain hardware date stays out. I don't think this is borderline.
- **Part 3 passes.** It names 2026.
- **Part 4 is coverage only.** There are no first-person words on this page. The run says Atlan was later dropped from the roadmap for a chip called Thor; I didn't check that, and it doesn't affect admission.
- **Not recorded.** Two recorded files come from the same day: Hyperion 8 in Jaguar Land Rover cars by 2025, and in Mercedes cars by 2024. Both are about Hyperion 8, not Hyperion 9 or the Atlan chip.
